title: Solo dev, day 1 of the Epic AI MegaJam: 400+ commits with Opus 5.5, Codex, and more
author: anotherbuilddev
selftext:
Last week I posted some beginner tips for making games with AI. and his week I joined the Epic AI MegaJam.

I’m solo. When the jam started at midnight I spent one hour setting things up, then let the agents run overnight. Opus 5.5 runs the main chat, Sonnet 5.5 does the individual pieces, and Codex made the concept art and the Blender models. I did part-time support on it throughout the day.

Day 1 numbers, from my local logs (I did use Fable 5.2 for some stuff as well):

* 400+ commits on main
* about 9.1M output tokens on Claude Code (about 2.4B more read from cache)
* 363 Codex sessions, about 176M tokens
* Claude Ultra plan at 50% of the weekly limit, nothing extra spent

What got built: enemy variants, 19 Rewrites (the upgrades), painted skies and atmosphere for each mission, new ships generated with Rodin, DLSS and ray tracing options, and a lot more. The workflow thing that helped most was critic loops. Separate agents whose only job is to play the game and find problems (regressions, balance, UI, VFX), then the builders fix what they found.

The video is the AI flying its own game, so it’s an early build with a lot of placeholder shapes.

If you’ve been on the fence about the jam: the AI partners are giving entrants free tokens, and you might still be able to claim some if you enter. The jam runs until Sunday night, check the itch page for what’s still available.

comments.author: anotherbuilddev
comments.body: What can I be doing better? The game, the workflow, anything.

comments.author: BudgeSoftGames
comments.body:
I am fascinated that devs are able to use AI like this.  I can't.  

My process is one prompt at a time, and is basically steering all day long.  If agents are running for 20 minutes that's a long time.

It's one thing if you have AI writing a code base/API/etc. but visual/audio assets, and game mechanics.  I can't see AI every getting that right w/o a lot of hand holding.  

Very interesting stuff.  Reminds me of a game I wrote for Oculus VR about 5 years ago.  Took me month and months and sold zero copies.. ha ha.  

[https://youtu.be/V6N64kWkSFc](https://youtu.be/V6N64kWkSFc)

replies.author: anotherbuilddev
replies.body: I started one prompt at a time a couple years ago, this became more natural over time. You do need to choose where to spend your focus!

replies.author: anotherbuilddev
replies.body: Your game is really cool, I think there just are not a huge audience of us out there for this sort of thing. Or we only need so many. Would have taken me a long time to build what you built if I didn’t have LLMs

replies.author: TheCrucibleMC
replies.body:
I think this is where you naturally evolve to. you start with one prompt at a time then it turns into enough work to justify multiple sessions but then you get tired of managing multiple sessions, so you start Coordinator session.

some days with that Coordinator session it is one prompt at a time when you’re really focused on the details, but sometimes you have a very detailed plan upfront that can be orchestrated across those sessions without any human activity

one of the most fun parts for me is actually getting the workflow optimized to a deeper level and every additional optimization is awesome to watch.

I started with making a super custom (no mod required) Minecraft server and now am working on my first full game. The entire thing becomes a personalized pipeline that I’m sure will help if I ever make a second game

replies.author: mirageofstars
replies.body: Well, the AI tools are also getting better. And the more AI game dev you do the more harnesses you'll hav etc speed things up.

replies.author: Bonelessgummybear
replies.body:
If you have a good setup and plan then it's a lot easier to trust AI to build overnight and unsupervised. When the game jam started at 11pm my time, I quickly built the grey box and play tested til 2am until I was satisfied. Then we built out some design docs, blueprints, and other tasks, grilled me on specifics. What's approved and not approved to do, then CronCreate heartbeat on a 30min interval. 

You get to wake up to a report, review and make your tweaks then wrap up. Start a new session. I like to restart my PC after an overnight run after all the commits are done. I've been using Fable 5.2 to orchestrate Haiku agents. Only 70% Fable usage after 36 hours, 39% weekly (all models). I have a reset ready as well for the Jam.

comments.author: Gothicawakening
comments.body:
> Separate agents who's only job is to play the game..

I'm curious how your workflow there looks, how many agents for a simple Play -> Review, for example UI related. Does the agent playing comment on UX mostly, and another for UI, or is one doing it all?

replies.author: anotherbuilddev
replies.body: Depends on what I am looking for. I find I have to do the UX myself more often and for the critic review loops on UI it is better with consistency and functionality than other stuff.

comments.author: Bonelessgummybear
comments.body: I'm very excited, this is my 1st game jam and I'm cooking hard. Im pretty surprised what I've got done so far in the past 36 hours. Unreal Engine has been great to work with for my game idea

replies.author: anotherbuilddev
replies.body: That's awesome. I've been making games for 20+ years and it has never been as much fun as it is now. Before you could have fun in making part of a game work quickly but now you can have fun making an entire game work quickly.

comments.author: SoundSoftWorks
comments.body: Amazing pace! How quickly did you exhaust your Fable usage?

replies.author: anotherbuilddev
replies.body:
Still only used 36% of fable so far. I am only using it on targeted areas. It is sort of like managing a team and knowing what tasks are overkill for your senior engineers vs. what a junior engineer can handle.

If the lower models fail to do a good enough job at something I'll have a better model do the work itself.
